title: Demonstrate an understanding of selecting the appropriate sites for growing grapes

lessons.title: Climate and the vineyard site
lessons.html:
Climate and the vineyard site

A vine can live and bear grapes for 25 years or more. If it is planted in the wrong place, the farm will have problems for all those years. That is why choosing the site is very important.

In South Africa, most wine grapes grow in the Western Cape, for example around Stellenbosch, Paarl, Worcester, Robertson and the Swartland. Table grapes and raisins also grow along the Orange River in the Northern Cape and in other areas.

What grapes need from the climate

  • Warm, dry summers: sun ripens the grapes and makes sugar.
  • Cool winters: vines rest (are dormant) in winter. Cold helps them bud evenly in spring.
  • Not too much rain at harvest: rain on ripe grapes causes rot and splitting.
  • No late frost: frost in spring can kill young shoots.
  • No hail: hail damages leaves and bunches.

Things that change the climate on one farm

  • Slope direction (aspect): in South Africa, slopes facing north get more sun and are warmer. Slopes facing south are cooler.
  • Height (altitude): higher places are cooler.
  • Low places: cold air flows down and collects in valleys and hollows. These frost pockets are bad for vines.
  • Wind: strong wind, such as the south-easter, can break shoots and dry out leaves. Wind breaks may be needed.
  • Closeness to the sea: sea breezes cool vineyards in the afternoon.

Why this matters

Different cultivars need different conditions. Cooler sites often suit cultivars such as Sauvignon Blanc. Warmer sites suit cultivars that need more heat to ripen. The farm manager matches the cultivar to the site.

lessons.title: Soil, water and other site checks
lessons.html:
Soil, water and other site checks

Soil

Vine roots can grow deep, a metre or more if the soil allows. A good vineyard soil:

  • is deep enough for roots to grow;
  • drains well, so water does not stand around the roots after rain;
  • is not too salty;
  • has no hard layer (such as a clay pan or rock) close to the surface, or the layer can be broken up when preparing the soil.

To check the soil, the farm digs soil profile pits (holes about as deep as a person) across the site and takes samples to a laboratory. The results show the soil type, depth, acidity (pH) and nutrients. Experts use them to plan soil preparation, lime and fertiliser.

Water

In many areas vines need irrigation, especially young vines. The site must have enough clean water. The farm must have the right to use that water under the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Water quality is checked too; salty water damages vines.

Other things to check

CheckWhy
Old vineyard on the landOld roots can carry viruses and nematodes
SlopeSteep slopes are hard to work and erode easily
Access roadsTrucks must reach the vineyard at harvest
Distance to the cellarPicked grapes must get to the cellar quickly
Neighbouring landSpray drift from other crops, or wild animals and birds that eat grapes

Your role

As a worker you may help dig profile pits, take soil samples and clear land. Dig pits safely: keep the sides sloped, never work alone in a deep pit, and keep soil heaps back from the edge so they do not fall in. Fill or fence the pits afterwards so people and animals do not fall in.

Key points

  • Vines stay for many years, so the site must be right from the start.
  • Grapes need warm, dry summers, cool winters and no late frost or hail at the wrong time.
  • Slope direction, height, low frost pockets and wind change the climate on a site.
  • Good vineyard soil is deep, well drained and not salty.
  • The site needs enough clean water and the legal right to use it.
